judgment.rationale: Both Indicators sit at BASIC 4 (rank 0) under Content Standard B4.2.2.2 'Solve one-step equations involving a symbol to represent an unknown number' (Algebra / Unknowns, Expressions and Equations), so the shared parentage alone is not decisive; the decision rests on statement text and Learning Components. B4.2.2.2.5 (second) states the general modelling routine — 'Identify the unknown in a problem', 'Represent the problem with an equation', 'Solve the problem concretely, pictorially or symbolically' — i.e. the generic identify-model-solve cycle across multiple representations. B4.2.2.2.6 (first) applies that same cycle to a narrower, more demanding case: a given addition or subtraction problem set in a 'part-part-whole' or comparison context, represented and solved specifically with a symbol for the unknown. Proficiency in identifying the unknown and writing an equation with flexible concrete/pictorial/symbolic solution methods plausibly supports success in the contextualised symbolic part-part-whole/comparison task, giving a substantive same-rank generality-to-application direction from the second SFI to the first rather than mere repetition. Code order (.5 before .6) and page proximity are treated as weak corroboration only. Confidence is moderated because both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted evidence items each) and same-rank direction is inferred from text rather than an explicit sequence statement.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 Indicators (rank 1, identical canonical coordinate) sharing the parent Content Standard B5.1.1.3 ('factors, multiples ... composite, even, odd and prime numbers from 1 to 100') within Strand 1 Number / Counting, Representation & Cardinality. B5.1.1.3.3 asks learners to classify even and odd numbers 1-100 via twos arrays, while B5.1.1.3.1 asks them to identify factors of whole numbers 1-100; their LCs ('arrays', 'even numbers', 'odd numbers', '1 to 100' vs 'factors', 'whole numbers') show genuine conceptual coherence around divisibility/array structure of numbers to 100, with the twos-array test being a concrete instance of factor reasoning. However, the two are same-rank complementary indicators and the bounded evidence does not substantively establish that proficiency in one is developmentally needed for the other in either direction (code ordering and shared parent are not semantic evidence), so a symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and ancestors carry merge/audit context, which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Same-grain Indicator pair, both resolved to Grade coordinate 'BASIC 5' (rank 1) and both children of Content Standard B5.1.3.1 'Demonstrate understanding of strategies for comparing, adding, subtracting and multiplying fractions' in Sub-Strand 3 'Number: Fractions'. B5.1.3.1.1 ('Determine equivalent fractions of given fractions') and B5.1.3.1.6 ('Use models to explain the result of multiplying a fraction by whole number') are substantively coherent complementary fraction-sense skills within the same BASIC 5 fraction-operations programme: equivalence/renaming and model-based interpretation of fraction multiplication mutually reinforce understanding of fractional quantity. This is more than word or code overlap, so canonical relatesTo is warranted. buildsTowards is not chosen: the endpoints share the same rank, and the only supplied signals are shared ancestry, a weak shared code prefix (B5.1.3.1), weak rank proximity (gap 0) and trivial token/trigram overlap ('of', fraction substrings); no bounded excerpt shows that determining equivalent fractions is required by, or measurably enables, modelling multiplication of a fraction by a whole number (that skill rests chiefly on unit-fraction/repeated-addition reasoning). Exemplar evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted source-evidence items each), so a developmental claim would rest on reconstructed content; confidence is moderate for the same reason. All endpoint, ancestor and request-wide audit/merge/code-context and truncation warnings are retained.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 Content Standards (same grain, same rank 1) under Sub-Strand 3: Geometric Reasoning within Strand 3: Geometry and Measurement. B5.3.4.1 asks learners to describe the position of objects in space using the cardinal points, while B5.3.4.2 asks them to perform a single transformation (reflection) on a 2D shape. They share coherent spatial-sense content — describing location/direction in a plane and mapping a shape to its image in a plane — so they reinforce each other conceptually. However, the bounded evidence (no Learning Components on either SFI; source evidence truncated with 24 omitted items each) shows no substantive dependency: cardinal-point positional language is not required to reflect a 2D shape, and the same-rank placement provides no developmental ordering. Adjacent codes, one-page proximity, and generic trigram overlap ('ing','ion','tio') are not semantic direction evidence, so a symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (same statement-type grain, rank 0) under the same perimeter Content Standard B4.3.3.1 in Sub-Strand 'Measurement- (Perimeter and Area)'. B4.3.3.1.2 establishes measuring and recording perimeter of regular and irregular shapes in cm and m; B4.3.3.1.4 requires constructing several different rectangles for a given perimeter in cm/m to show many shapes share one perimeter. The latter is a substantively more complex, inverse/generative task that presupposes reliable measurement and recording of perimeter in the same units, so proficiency in the measuring indicator supports success in the construction indicator. Direction at equal grade rank is supported by this task-complexity relationship (measure/record as enabling skill for construct-to-a-given-perimeter), not merely by shared parent or code prefix.
